messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mohammad is a 41-year-old Middle Eastern man who works at a fast food restaurant. He has been single for several years and describes his life as somewhat isolated. About six months ago, Mohammad witnessed a traumatic event at work when he saw one of his colleagues being violently attacked by an agitated customer during the lunch rush. The incident was particularly distressing because it happened right before him, and despite calling out to his colleague to get help, no one came to their aid in time. Since then, Mohammad has been struggling with a number of symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily life. One of the most prominent triggers for him is being criticized or corrected. This fear is rooted in the memory of feeling helpless and ignored during the attack; he recalls how even his attempts to call out for help were met with no response. Now, any form of criticism at work sends him into a state of heightened anxiety. The same time of day when the incident occurred also triggers intense feelings of dread and vulnerability. Loud noises have become another significant trigger for Mohammad. He vividly remembers the sounds of shattering glass and shouting during the attack, which has made unexpected or loud sounds extremely distressing. Any sudden noise now immediately makes him feel as if he is back in that moment, and his heart races with fear. Mohammad's sense of safety has drastically narrowed since the incident. He only feels secure within a very limited number of places, primarily his home and work. Outside these areas, he experiences constant vigilance, always on edge. This hyper-vigilance extends to everyday activities; when something takes longer than expected, he assumes that something bad is happening. For example, if he hears footsteps approaching while waiting in line at the grocery store, his mind immediately jumps to worst-case scenarios. At work, Mohammad's symptoms have started to affect his job performance and relationships with colleagues. His fear of being criticized leads him to avoid taking on new tasks or responsibilities that might result in mistakes. This has made him hesitant to engage fully in team activities, leading to a sense of isolation from his coworkers. He has also developed a habit of avoiding any conversations about the past incident at work, which makes it difficult for him to form deeper connections with others. The cumulative effect of these triggers and threats is a cycle of heightened anxiety that Mohammad finds increasingly hard to manage. Each trigger reinforces his belief that he is not safe outside of his limited "safe zone," leading to further avoidance behaviors and increased vigilance. This constant state of alertness has taken its toll on his mental health, making him feel constantly on edge. What finally brought Mohammad to seek help was a recent incident at work where a customer yelled at him for a minor mistake. The sound of the yelling triggered a panic attack that left him feeling overwhelmed and helpless once again. He recognizes now that these symptoms are interfering with his ability to live a normal life, and he is most afraid of becoming completely isolated. Mohammad hopes therapy can help him regain some sense of safety and control over his daily experiences. Through this journey, Mohammad has come to understand the deep-seated fears and anxieties triggered by specific moments from the traumatic event. The goal now is to break the cycle of avoidance and vigilance, helping him feel safer in a broader range of environments without reliving the trauma every time he encounters similar triggers.
